# Clover Devices—Technical Specifications

This page documents the technical specifications for Clover point-of-sale (POS) hardware devices across North America, Europe, and Latin America.

## Key Announcement
**End-of-App-Update (EOAU) for Gen 1 devices in the US on March 30, 2026.** Gen 1 devices (Clover Station C010, Mobile C020/C021, Mini C030/C031, Flex C041/C042) reach EOAU on **May 15, 2026**. App developers must review compatibility and plan upgrades.

## Clover Station Models
- **Station Solo** — All-in-one POS with 14" HD display, built-in printer, cash drawer. OS: Android 10 (API 29). Snapdragon 660, 2GB RAM/16GB Flash. EMV + MSR. Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G LTE. Fingerprint reader.
- **Station Solo (International)** — Similar to Solo with 5MP camera for 1D/2D barcode scanning, 3.5mm audio jack.
- **Station Duo 2** — Dual-screen: 14" merchant + 8" customer. Android 10. Dual 5MP cameras with Zebra scanning. Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G/LTE. Accessibility features.
- **Station Duo (formerly Station Pro)** — Dual-screen with 14" merchant + 7" customer. Android 8.1 (upgradable to 10). EMV, NFC, MSR. 5MP cameras.
- **Station (2018)** — 14" HD display, fingerprint reader. Android 7.0. Snapdragon 810, 3GB RAM/16GB Flash. Up to 4-hour battery. Ethernet, Wi-Fi.

## Clover Mini & Compact
- **Mini 3** — 8" screen, Android 10. Snapdragon octa-core, 2GB RAM/16GB Flash. Internal thermal printer. EMV, NFC, MSR. Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 4G/LTE.
- **Mini 2** — 7" display, Android 8.1 (upgradable to 10). Snapdragon 660, 2GB RAM/16GB Flash. Internal printer.
- **Compact** — 3.62" IPS LCD, physical keypad with accessibility features. Android 13. 2GB RAM/16GB Flash. 5MP camera. Internal thermal printer (58mm paper). PCI PTS 6.x. Dimensions: 7.4" x 2.9" x 3.4", 0.84 lbs.

## Clover Flex Models
- **Flex 4** — 5.99" IPS LCD, 1440x720. Android 13, API 33. 4GB RAM/64GB Flash. 5MP camera. EMV Contact/Contactless, MSR. 4G/LTE, WiFi, Bluetooth. Internal thermal printer. Wireless charging cradle.
- **Flex Pocket** — Slim, lightweight model. No built-in printer. Android 13. 4GB RAM/64GB Flash. USB Type C charging (no cradle). No wireless charging.
- **Flex 3** — 5.99" HD screen, Android 10. Snapdragon 660, 2GB RAM/16GB Flash. 5MP camera. Internal printer. 1D/2D barcode scanner with dedicated button.

## Clover Go (BYOD Solution)
- Bring-your-own-device mobile POS system using Clover Go app (iOS/Android).
- **Go Reader** — EMV-capable device paired via Bluetooth. Accepts swipe, dip, tap, NFC (Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay). 160 dip/130 contactless transactions per charge.
- **Go Dock** — Countertop mount with security lock and USB charging.
- **Clover Go SDK** — EMV Level 3 certified, available for iOS and Android integration.

## Receipt Printer Specifications
| Printer | Paper Length | Paper Width | Pixel Width |
|---------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| Station Duo/Station (2018)/Station Printer | 230 ft | 3 1/8 in | 576 px |
| Mini Internal | 85 ft | 2 1/4 in | 384 px |
| Flex Internal | 50 ft | 2 1/4 in | 384 px |
| Compact Internal | 50 ft | 2 1/4 in | 384 px |
| Star Micronics SP742ML Kitchen Printer | 100-165 ft | 3 in | N/A |

# Clover Station Duo vs Clover Flex: Which POS Hardware Is Better for Your Business?

* By Sandra Larson
* [No Comments](https://geekvibesnation.com/clover-station-duo-vs-clover-flex-which-pos-hardware-is-better-for-your-business/#respond)

* [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fgeekvibesnation.com%2Fclover-station-duo-vs-clover-flex-which-pos-hardware-is-better-for-your-business%2F&t=Clover+Station+Duo+vs+Clover+Flex%3A+Which+POS+Hardware+Is+Better+for+Your+Business%3F "Share on Facebook")

* [Reddit](https://reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgeekvibesnation.com%2Fclover-station-duo-vs-clover-flex-which-pos-hardware-is-better-for-your-business%2F&title=Clover+Station+Duo+vs+Clover+Flex%3A+Which+POS+Hardware+Is+Better+for+Your+Business%3F "Share on Reddit")

![A man uses a self-service kiosk at an airport, holding his phone and interacting with the touchscreen.](https://cdn.geekvibesnation.com/wp-media-folder-geek-vibes-nation/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/AdobeStock_561638770-1024x683.jpeg)

Wrong hardware kills your checkout flow. The [Clover Station Duo](https://smartpaymentsolutions.us/clover-station-duo/) and the Clover Flex sit at opposite ends of the same ecosystem — one is bolted to a counter, the other fits in a server’s apron pocket — and picking the wrong one means either overpaying for hardware you don’t need or throttling your operation with a device that can’t keep up. So let’s break down where each one actually works, where it breaks, and how to make the call without guessing.

## The Clover Ecosystem: What You’re Actually Buying Into

Clover runs on a closed-loop model. Hardware, software, and payment processing are bundled — you don’t mix and match with third-party terminals the way you might with a generic Android device. That’s a feature if you want a tight stack. It’s a constraint if you already have a processor you love.

Monthly service fees vary by plan and partner, typically ranging from $25 to $45 depending on the feature set you activate. Hardware is priced separately. **Factor both numbers into your total cost of ownership before you sign anything.**

The platform covers inventory management, employee scheduling, reporting, and kitchen display integration. Whether you need all of that depends on your operation size and type.

## Clover Station Duo: The Countertop Workhorse

Two screens. One counter. That’s the core concept. The Station Duo runs dual 10.1-inch displays — one facing your staff, one facing the customer. The customer-facing screen handles tip prompts, digital receipts, loyalty enrollment, and payment confirmation without your cashier rotating a device or shouting totals across the counter.

**Hardware specs that matter operationally:**

* Dual 10.1-inch touchscreens (staff + customer-facing)
* Fixed countertop setup — requires power adapter, not battery-dependent
* Supports optional integrated receipt printer
* Connects to kitchen display systems natively
* Supports multi-tenant configurations for larger or multi-location deployments

Hardware-only pricing runs $1,499–$1,899. That’s the entry point before software, peripherals, or installation.

During a busy lunch rush at a quick-service counter, the dual-screen layout cuts transaction time — customers see their order total, tap to tip, and confirm payment without waiting for a staff handoff. **The customer-facing display is the real productivity multiplier here, not just a cosmetic feature.**

Where it fits: full-service retail, restaurant front-of-house counters, coffee shops with steady foot traffic, and any fixed checkout point where you need integrated inventory and kitchen display firing simultaneously. If you’re running a multi-station setup across a larger venue, the Duo’s multi-tenant support gives you the flexibility to scale without switching platforms.

Where it breaks: anywhere you need to move. The Duo is tethered. Power goes out, cord gets kicked, counter gets reconfigured — your checkout stops. No battery fallback.

## Clover Flex: Mobile POS Without the Compromises

The Flex is a 5.5-inch handheld with a built-in card reader, NFC, and Bluetooth. It runs on a rechargeable battery rated for up to 12 hours of continuous use. It connects via Wi-Fi or cellular. That’s the whole pitch — take payments wherever your customer is standing.

For tableside checkout in a full-service restaurant, the Flex removes the dead time between “check please” and card return. A server carries the terminal to the table, the customer taps or dips, done. No card leaves the customer’s hand. That matters for both speed and fraud optics.

At a weekend farmers market or pop-up retail event, the Flex runs on cellular if your venue Wi-Fi is unreliable (which it usually is at those events, honestly). Battery life across a full market day is realistic — assuming you start with a full charge and aren’t running video-heavy apps in the background.

**Scenarios where the Flex earns its keep:**

* Tableside payment in full-service restaurants
* Line-busting during peak hours — take the terminal to the queue
* Pop-up retail and outdoor events
* Delivery drivers collecting payment at the door
* Curbside pickup without a fixed terminal

Hardware starts at $799–$999. Lighter upfront investment, but check your service plan — the Flex on a stripped-down plan loses some reporting depth you’d get on the full Duo stack.

The catch: the Flex does not natively integrate with kitchen display systems. If your kitchen workflow depends on order tickets firing directly from the POS to a KDS, the Flex alone won’t close that loop. You’d need a hybrid setup — which brings us to the combination question.

For operations that want mobile payment capability without sacrificing kitchen integration, pairing a Duo at the counter with a [Clover Flex POS](https://smartpaymentsolutions.us/clover-flex/) for tableside or curbside creates a workable hybrid stack. The Duo anchors your fixed checkout and KDS; the Flex handles everything that moves.

## Direct Comparison: Where the Decision Actually Lives

**Mobility vs. fixed checkout:** If your checkout point doesn’t move, the Duo’s dual-screen layout and peripheral integration justify the price gap. If your checkout follows the customer, the Flex is the only logical choice.

**Kitchen integration:** Duo wins here. Flex doesn’t natively trigger KDS. In a restaurant environment where ticket accuracy and fire timing matter, that’s not a small gap.

**Customer-facing display:** The Duo’s 10.1-inch customer screen handles tip prompts and payment confirmation in a way that the Flex’s 5.5-inch single screen can’t replicate at the same visual scale. For high-volume counters, that customer screen reduces friction and staff intervention per transaction.

**Upfront hardware cost:** Flex runs roughly $700 less at the low end. For a single-location pop-up or a lean mobile operation, that delta is meaningful. For a permanent retail or restaurant counter, the Duo’s operational output typically offsets the price difference over time — though exact ROI varies by transaction volume and deployment.

**Multi-location or enterprise use:** Station Duo supports multi-tenant configurations. Flex is single-tenant. If you’re scaling across locations and need centralized management, the Duo’s architecture handles that; the Flex doesn’t.

## How to Make the Call for Your Operation

Ask three questions before you order anything.

First: **does your checkout point move?** If the answer is yes — even occasionally — the Flex belongs in your setup. If it never moves, the Duo’s fixed architecture works harder for you.

Second: **do you need kitchen display integration?** If you’re running a restaurant with a back-of-house KDS, the Duo is not optional — it’s the device that closes that workflow. The Flex won’t replace it.

Third: **what’s your realistic transaction volume at a fixed counter?** High-volume counters benefit from the dual-screen layout because it speeds up customer-side interactions. Lower-volume or mobile contexts don’t need that infrastructure.

Edge cases worth flagging: if your power goes out mid-shift, the Duo goes dark — no battery fallback. Keep that in mind for venues with unstable power. On the Flex side, if cellular connectivity drops in a basement event space and your Wi-Fi is patchy, you’re potentially processing offline — verify your partner’s offline fallback policy before you rely on it.

**For most food and beverage operations:** a Duo at the counter plus one or two Flex units for tableside or line-busting is the configuration that covers the most ground without redundancy. For pure retail with a fixed counter, the Duo alone handles the job. For pop-ups, delivery, or single-operator mobile businesses, the Flex is sufficient and the Duo is overkill.

The hardware decision is operational, not aspirational. Buy what your actual workflow demands in 2026 — not what looks impressive on a spec sheet.

# Why the Clover Station Duo is the Ultimate All-In-One POS System

By [Danny Gagliardi](https://mondopayments.com/author/mondop-admin/)[No Comments](https://mondopayments.com/why-the-clover-station-duo-is-the-ultimate-all-in-one-pos-system/#respond)

Having a proper point of sales (POS) system makes it easier to manage your business. An effective payment terminal simplifies daily business tasks and helps generate higher revenues. Advanced POS systems such as the [Clover Flex](https://clover.com/flex) and the [Clover Station Duo](https://www.clover.com/station-duo) can further attract new customers and increase business sales.

The [Clover Station Duo](https://www.mondopayments.com/products/clover-station-duo) is the ultimate all-in-one POS system that centralizes the management of your business operations. It works as the central hub of any retail business to attract and engage customers. No matter what type of retailer you are, learn how this Clover terminal is everything your business needs to grow.

### What Is the Clover Station Duo?

Clover is a major player in the industry for several reasons. It is considered the best POS system for retailers because of its highly competitive products and incredibly intuitive system. Today, Clover offers a wide range of POS software and hardware solutions for any business type, giving every owner the ability to upgrade as the business expands.

The Clover Station Duo is a two-screen complete POS system that allows you to run your entire business and allows your customers to initiate payments. It offers a wide range of software and hardware applications with endless possibilities. Each device comes with almost everything you need, such as a customer-facing terminal, touchscreen display, barcode scanner, receipt printer, cash drawer, and other software features.

### Clover Station Duo Terminal: Technical Specifications

Clover Station Duo is Clover’s latest hardware offering. The main difference between the Station Solo and Station Duo is the add-on customer-facing terminal. This terminal also has the following powerful features:

* 14-in merchant-facing display screen
* 7-in customer-facing terminal
* 2 GB RAM and 16 GB flash memory
* WiFi and ethernet connectivity, and also 4G/LTE ready
* Comes with a power cable and a LAN cable for the power source
* Has four USB ports (Type A)
* P501 receipt printer
* Barcode scanner
* Cash drawer

### Clover Station Duo Features

This fast and powerful POS system does everything from inventory management to running reports and managing your people. Here are some of the best features of the Clover Station Duo:

#### Integrated Accessories

The Station Duo has integrated accessories, such as the standard receipt printer and handheld bar code scanners. You can also upgrade to a label printer or a kitchen printer. Additionally, it includes integrated and non-integrated weight scales.

#### LTE Enabled

The Clover Station Duo with LTE capability gives you added connectivity support to your mobile network. Additionally, you only pay when you use it.

#### Enhanced Security

The Station Duo provides data protection and enhanced security with fingerprint and NFC login. It also offers transaction tokenization and encryption and PCI PTS 5.0 PED w/P2PE readiness.

#### Online Ordering

We all know that online ordering is crucial in doing business. Station Duo offers the Clover dashboard to configure your online menu easily. Additionally, you can set up social media links and QR codes to guide your customers to your online menu. You can also customize your wait times and business operating hours in the Clover Dashboard.

#### Virtual Clover Terminal and Online Payments

If you want to process card transactions for your client and don’t have your payment terminal near you, don’t worry. Go to the dashboard, login, and process a card-not-present transaction. This virtual terminal offers convenience and flexibility in processing payments wherever you are.

#### Clover App Market

The Clover App Market is built for small businesses to run businesses better. It has over 150 applications that you can integrate with the Station Duo to turn it into a versatile and multitasking machine. Applications such as time clock management, employee scheduling, and Quickbooks integrations are some of the business apps offered by the Clover App Market.

#### Is Clover Station Duo Right For You?

Now, you’ve learned what the powerful features of Station Duo are. You might be thinking now if this Clover POS system is what you need for your business. Well, with the Station Duo, you can get everything done using only one system, and it’s great for the following types of businesses:

* Restaurants: The Station Duo is perfect for all types of restaurants, such as quick-service and counter-service restaurants.
* Retail: It’s the perfect device for retails, such as apparel, sports shop, specialist shop, convenience stores, and grocery stores that process payments at a counter.
* Services: Some examples of businesses that can benefit from the Station Duo include dental clinics, beauty salons, accounting offices, car dealerships, and other such types of companies.

### Grow Your Business With Clover Station Duo and Mondo Payments

The retail landscape is dynamically changing, and as a business owner, you don’t want to be left behind due to your outdated systems. At Mondo Payments, we can help you understand the importance of these solutions and upgrade your operations. We supply solutions to future proof your retail business.

# Square Hardware Comparison: Which Square POS Device Is Best for Your Business?

Written By [![](data:image/avif;base64,)
![Agatha Aviso](https://cdn.fitsmallbusiness.com/83a5fd37f77090803ed81d016944f064d3dee3e137b20923943d4ceec94acb2a.jpg?w=64)

Agatha Aviso](/author/agatha-aviso/)

Apr 8, 2026

 ·   15 minute read

I’ve tested Square across different small business setups, and one thing is consistent: the right hardware depends on how you sell. Your checkout flow, sales volume, and whether you’re mobile or stationary matter more than the upfront price. A weekend market vendor can run with a simple reader, while a busy retail store needs a structured counter setup to keep lines moving.

In this guide, I break down each Square device, show you what it actually does in real use, and help you choose the best fit for your business.

| Square hardware | Best for | Price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [**Square Reader for magstripe**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-reader-for-magstripe-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Swipe payments (very small sellers, backup use) | Free for first reader; $10 for every succeeding purchase |
| [**Square Reader for contactless and chip**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-reader-for-contactless-and-chip-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Basic payments (mobile sellers, services) | $59 |
| [**Square Terminal**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-terminal-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | All-in-one POS (cafes, small shops) | $299 |
| [**Square Handheld**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-handheld-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Mobile POS (restaurants, line-busting) | From $399 |
| [**Square Stand**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-stand-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Countertop POS (retail stores) | $149 (iPad sold separately) |
| [**Square Register**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-register-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Full POS system (high-volume retail) | $899 |
| [**Square Kiosk**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-kiosk-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Self-service ordering (quick-service restos) | $149 (iPad sold separately) |

Square’s POS software is free to start, with paid upgrades available depending on your business needs. It uses a [**unified pricing model**](https://squareup.com/us/en/press/unified-pricing-and-packagin) with three plans — Square Free, Square Plus, and Square Premium — so your POS, payments, inventory, and customer tools all run on the same system without needing extra integrations.

Square earns revenue through payment processing, with standard rates typically starting at 2.6% + 15 cents per in-person transaction. **Square hardware is also proprietary**, meaning it only works with Square POS. While you can’t use it with other systems, the benefit is a more streamlined setup where everything is designed to work together out of the box.

## Square hardware comparison table

| Setup type | Built-in screen | Built-in printer | Standout feature |

| [**Square Reader for contactless and chip**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-reader-for-contactless-and-chip-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | Mobile (phone/tablet required) | ✕ | ✕ | Accepts tap, chip, and mobile wallets |
| [**Square Terminal**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-terminal-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | All-in-one device | ✔ | ✔ | Built-in receipt printer |
| [**Square Handheld**](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-handheld-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) | All-in-one mobile device | ✔ | ✕ | Take orders and payments anywhere |

## Which Square hardware is best for your business?

* If you just need to accept quick and simple card payments, use Square Reader.
* If you sell at pop-ups or need a mobile setup, use Square Terminal or Square Handheld.
* If you run a retail checkout counter, use Square Stand or Square Register.
* If you manage a high-volume retail store, use Square Register.
* If you operate a restaurant or need tableside service, use Square Handheld.
* If you want customers to place their own orders, use Square Kiosk.
* If you want the simplest all-in-one setup with minimal accessories, use Square Terminal.
* If you’re just starting out and want the lowest upfront cost, use Square Reader.

## Square Reader (magstripe vs contactless and chip): Best for low-cost card payments

| **Who should use it:**Solo, occasional or on-the-go sellers, service providers, and new businesses testing demand. | **Pricing:**Free for the first order; $10 for every succeeding purchase for the Square Reader for magstripe; $59 or $21 per month with financing for the Square Reader for contactless and chip | [Buy Square Reader](https://link.technologyadvice.com/r/square-reader-for-contactless-and-chip-fsb-square-hardware-comparison) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How Square Reader works   Both versions connect to your phone or tablet and use the Square POS app to process payments. You enter the sale on your device, then the customer completes the payment on the reader. Square Reader for magstripe and Square Reader for contactless and chip devices side by side  Square Reader for magstripe (left) and Square Reader for contactless and chip (right).  * The **magstripe reader** plugs into your phone (or connects via adapter) and only accepts swipe payments. * The **contactless and chip reader** connects via Bluetooth and supports tap, chip, and mobile wallets like Apple Pay.   In practice, setup is quick for both, but the contactless version is noticeably smoother for everyday use since most customers prefer tapping or inserting cards. You don’t need to buy Square hardware right away. Many small businesses start with a phone or tablet and upgrade as their sales grow.

* Have low sales volume
* Sell on the go (markets, services, pop-ups)
* Want the lowest upfront cost

Invest in Square hardware if you:

* Process many transactions daily
* Have employees using your POS
* Want faster checkout and fewer errors
* Need a more professional, fixed setup

Dedicated hardware like Square Terminal, Stand, or Register helps streamline operations and reduces reliance on personal devices.

## Square hardware limitations to know before you buy

Square hardware is easy to start with, but most businesses will need to upgrade as they grow. There are a few tradeoffs to keep in mind before you commit.

* **Some setups require extra accessories:** Devices like Square Stand and Register often need a receipt printer, cash drawer, or scanner to function as a complete POS. These add to your total cost.
* **Entry-level hardware can slow you down:** Square Reader works well for occasional sales, but it can slow checkout during busy periods since everything runs through your phone.
* **Not all devices are built for mobility:** Square Register and Kiosk are designed for fixed setups. If you need flexibility, you’ll need a mobile device like Square Handheld or Terminal.
* **Some systems are better for simple workflows:** Devices like Square Terminal are great for straightforward transactions but may feel limited if you need advanced inventory tracking or multi-register setups.

## What to consider when choosing Square hardware

Choosing Square hardware comes down to how your business runs day to day. Start with how you sell, then match your setup to your workflow, staff, and sales volume.

* **How you sell:** If you sell on the go, you’ll need a mobile setup like Square Reader, Terminal, or Handheld. If you sell at a counter, Square Stand or Register is a better fit.
* **Your transaction volume:** Low-volume businesses can get by with simpler hardware. Higher-volume stores need faster systems like Square Register to keep lines moving.
* **Mobility vs fixed setup:** If you need to move around (restaurants, events), choose portable devices. For a dedicated checkout area, go with a countertop system.
* **Your budget (including accessories):** Don’t just look at the device price. Factor in the cost of printers, drawers, and other add-ons when comparing options.
* **Your future growth:** Choose hardware that can scale with your business. It’s often worth investing in a more capable setup early if you expect to grow quickly.

What is the best Square hardware for a small business?

The best Square hardware depends on how you run your business. For most small businesses, Square Terminal is the easiest all-in-one option since it includes a screen, card reader, and receipt printer in a single device. Which Square device has a built-in receipt printer?

Square Terminal is the only Square device with a built-in receipt printer. All other hardware, including Square Stand and Square Register, requires a separate printer if you want to provide printed receipts.

Do I need an iPad for Square Stand?

Yes, Square Stand requires an iPad to function. The Stand acts as a dock and card reader, while the Square POS app runs on the iPad itself, so you’ll need to purchase or already have a compatible iPad.

Can I use Square without buying hardware?

Yes, you can use Square without buying dedicated hardware by running the Square POS app on your phone or tablet. You can manually enter payments or pair your device with a Square Reader, which is the lowest-cost way to start accepting card payments.

What accessories do I need for Square POS?

Most Square setups require a few accessories to function as a complete POS system. Common add-ons include a receipt printer for printed receipts, a cash drawer if you accept cash, and a barcode scanner for retail inventory. Depending on your setup, you may also need mounts, stands, or networking equipment to keep your system stable and reliable.

## FAQs

### Is Square a good POS system?

Square stands out as an excellent POS system due to its transparent pricing and user-friendly interface, making it an optimal choice for small to medium-sized businesses. Notably, some large enterprises also leverage its services.

### What's the difference between Square and Square restaurant?

Square and Square Restaurant differ primarily in their specialized features tailored for restaurant businesses. While Square offers a comprehensive POS solution for various industries, Square Restaurant focuses specifically on restaurant management needs.

### What is included in a Square Stand?

The Square Stand restaurant POS hardware bundle includes a Square Stand, a cash drawer, and a receipt printer. Simply connect an iPad, download Square Point of Sale, and plug in the hardware to start processing payments effortlessly.

### Does Square Stand require Wi-Fi?

Square Stand operates seamlessly with Wi-Fi or cellular signal via your iPad. This ensures faster checkout experiences with integrated payment options such as chip reader (EMV) and contactless payments like tap cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, or Afterpay.

### What operating system does Square use?

Square POS is compatible with devices running Android 7 or higher. Ensure your device runs an updated version of the Square app, version 5 or higher for Android, to leverage its full functionalities.

### Is Square Register good for Restaurants?

Square for Restaurants, a comprehensive cloud-based POS system, is ideal for quick-service and full-service restaurants alike. It offers integration with kitchen display systems, customer loyalty programs, and staff management tools, enhancing operational efficiency.

### How much does a restaurant point of sale system cost?

Restaurant POS system costs vary, ranging from $0 to over $200 per month for cloud-based solutions. Additionally, hardware expenses start at around $1000 for legacy systems, making Square's transparent pricing a competitive choice.

### What is the downside of Square?

Despite its benefits, Square's processing fees might be a concern for some users. However, its transparent pricing model ensures clarity regarding the fees, making it easier to understand the costs associated with its services.

### What is the difference between Square Stand Gen 1 and Gen 2?

Square Stand Gen 2 features a sleek black finish and incorporates a built-in contactless and chip card reader, distinguishing it from the entirely white Gen 1. This upgrade enhances both aesthetics and functionality for users.

### What iPad is needed for Square POS?

Square POS is compatible with 10.2” and 10.5” iPads, providing flexibility in choosing the appropriate device for your restaurant POS station.

This is a product page for the **Square Stand Restaurant POS Station Kit - Black/White**, sold by eMerchant Authority for **$1,039.00** (in stock). It is a complete point-of-sale hardware bundle designed for hospitality and restaurant environments, including:

- **Square Stand** (compatible with iPad 10.2" 2019-2021, iPad Air 10.5" 2019, iPad Pro 10.5")
- **Square Reader for contactless and chip** plus Dock
- **16" Printer-Driven Cash Drawer** (stainless steel, 5 bill/8 coin compartments)
- **Ethernet Kitchen Printer** (4.7 LPS print speed)
- **USB Receipt Printer** (direct thermal, 250mm/s)
- **Kitchen Printer Paper** (25 rolls) and **Thermal Receipt Paper** (25 rolls)

Supported payment types include EMV chip cards, NFC contactless, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Samsung Pay, and magnetic-stripe cards. The page also includes a FAQ section covering Square POS system questions (compatibility, differences between Square vs. Square Restaurant, Gen 1 vs. Gen 2 differences, iPad requirements, and pricing). Additional related products from Clover, Verifone, and Ingenico are listed as cross-sells.

This analysis compares the three US market leaders in serving single-location restaurants and small chains through the Integrated Software Vendor (ISV) model: Square, Clover, and Toast. All three compete in the restaurant vertical and pursue similar growth strategies — expanding to more verticals, countries, omnichannel services, and larger chains. However, they differ significantly in their distribution models and starting points.

**Key Differences by Distribution Model:**
- **Toast** started with larger, single-location, table-service restaurants using a direct sales force. This creates a "flywheel" effect in metro areas, generating inbound demand. Toast has the highest US restaurant TPV and the most tailored, proprietary restaurant solutions.
- **Clover** started with smaller, counter-service restaurants using an indirect sales model through bank branches (especially Wells Fargo and PNC, which own 60% of their respective JVs) and ISOs/VARs. They leverage parent Fiserv for chain access.

# What Every Merchant Needs to Know About EMV & PCI Compliance in 2025

[Merchant Tips](/topic/merchant-tips)

With data breaches continuing to make headlines and consumer expectations around security at an all-time high, businesses that accept card payments can no longer afford to treat compliance as an afterthought. Whether you're running a boutique retail shop, a restaurant, or a growing ecommerce brand, understanding the fundamentals of EMV and PCI compliance is essential to protecting your revenue, your reputation, and your customers.

In 2025, compliance isn’t just about avoiding fines or ticking off a checklist—it’s about building trust and ensuring your business remains resilient in a fast-evolving payments landscape.

## What Is PCI Compliance?

**PCI compliance** refers to adherence to the [Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/standards/)—a set of security standards developed to protect cardholder data during and after a financial transaction.

Any U.S. business that processes, stores, or transmits credit card information is required to comply with these standards. PCI DSS is maintained by the PCI Security Standards Council and applies to all types of card transactions, from countertop terminals to online payments.

### Key Objectives of PCI DSS:

* Build and maintain a secure network
* Protect cardholder data
* Maintain a vulnerability management program
* Implement strong access control measures
* Regularly monitor and test networks
* Maintain an information security policy

## Why PCI Compliance Matters More in 2025

The risks surrounding card data are not hypothetical. According to industry analysts, [cyberattacks targeting small to mid-sized U.S. businesses have grown steadily](https://www.itsolutions-inc.com/guides/the-growing-threat-cyberattacks-on-small-and-medium-sized-businesses/), especially in retail and food service sectors where outdated point-of-sale (POS) systems are still in use.

In addition to potential fraud and customer churn, merchants who are not compliant with PCI DSS can face:

* Hefty non-compliance fees from payment processors
* Higher chargeback rates and penalties
* Legal exposure in the event of a data breach
* Damage to brand trust and customer loyalty

With increased consumer awareness of security risks, businesses that take proactive steps to protect customer data are far more likely to earn long-term trust and repeat business.

## Understanding EMV: A First Line of Defense

While PCI compliance focuses on a broad range of security best practices, **EMV**—which stands for Europay, Mastercard, and Visa—specifically refers to the technology behind chip-enabled credit and debit cards. EMV terminals use encrypted communication to verify card data, making it significantly harder for fraudsters to clone cards or skim information.

### Why EMV Still Matters:

* EMV chips generate dynamic data for each transaction, making them more secure than magnetic stripes.
* As of 2015, liability for fraudulent transactions has shifted to the merchant if they are not using an EMV-capable terminal.
* EMV adoption has led to a steep decline in counterfeit card fraud at physical points of sale.

Even in 2025, [EMV remains the standard for in-person transactions in the U.S.](https://www.tidalcommerce.com/learn/inside-the-emv-chip), and any merchant not using chip-enabled terminals is assuming unnecessary risk.

## What Merchants Need to Do to Stay PCI Compliant

Staying PCI compliant doesn’t have to be overwhelming, but it does require consistency and awareness. Here are the key steps most U.S. businesses need to follow:

### 1. **Determine Your Merchant Level**

Your PCI requirements depend on your volume of transactions. Smaller businesses (Level 3 or 4) typically complete a self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ), while larger businesses may require formal audits.

### 2. **Use a Secure POS and Payment Gateway**

One of the most critical components of PCI compliance is ensuring that your payment system is up to date. This includes:

* EMV-compliant terminals
* Point-to-point encryption (P2PE)
* Tokenization to secure cardholder data

Modern, cloud-based POS systems are often easier to secure than legacy systems, since they are built with encryption and security patches in mind.

### 3. **Segment and Secure Your Network**

If you’re accepting payments on the same network used for other business operations (like Wi-Fi or office printers), consider segmenting your network to isolate card data and reduce risk exposure.

### 4. **Complete the Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ)**

Most small and mid-sized businesses can meet their PCI obligations by completing an annual SAQ and conducting quarterly vulnerability scans through an approved scanning vendor (ASV).

### 5. **Train Employees on Security Protocols**

Even the most secure system can be compromised by human error. All staff members handling transactions should be trained in recognizing phishing attempts, securely handling devices, and following best practices for data security.

## Tokenization: Going Beyond PCI Compliance

While PCI DSS sets the minimum bar, many merchants choose to go further by adopting **tokenization**—a process that replaces sensitive card data with a unique token that cannot be used outside a specific system. This means even if a token is intercepted or accessed, it’s useless to attackers.

Benefits of tokenization include:

* Reduced scope of PCI DSS audits
* Improved security for stored cardholder data
* Enhanced customer trust
* Seamless recurring billing or loyalty features for repeat customers

Combined with encryption and EMV, tokenization forms a comprehensive defense strategy for modern payment environments.

## Common PCI Compliance Pitfalls to Avoid

Despite best intentions, some merchants fall short on compliance due to simple oversights. Here are some common mistakes to avoid:

* Using outdated terminals that don’t support EMV or encryption
* Storing full card numbers or CVVs on systems
* Not segmenting payment networks from other systems
* Failing to complete the annual SAQ
* Assuming ecommerce platforms handle 100% of PCI compliance (they don’t)

Regular reviews and working with knowledgeable payment providers can help you stay ahead of these issues.

## Conclusion: PCI Compliance and Security as a Business Advantage

In today’s environment, PCI compliance isn’t just about avoiding penalties—it’s about showing customers that you take their trust seriously. EMV, tokenization, and secure POS infrastructure all work together to create a safer, more resilient payments ecosystem.

That’s why we built our systems at **Tidal Commerce** to meet the highest security standards. We also offer direct assistance for completing your SAQ and identifying gaps in your existing setup.

args.summary:
This article from Tidal Commerce explains what merchants need to know about EMV and PCI compliance in 2025. PCI compliance refers to adhering to the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a set of security standards for protecting cardholder data. Any U.S. business processing, storing, or transmitting credit card information must comply. Key PCI DSS objectives include building a secure network, protecting cardholder data, maintaining vulnerability management, implementing access controls, monitoring networks, and maintaining a security policy.

Non-compliance can result in fines, higher chargebacks, legal exposure, and loss of customer trust. EMV technology (chip-enabled cards) generates dynamic data per transaction, making it harder to clone cards. Since 2015, merchants not using EMV-capable terminals bear liability for fraudulent transactions.

To stay PCI compliant, merchants should: (1) determine their merchant level based on transaction volume, (2) use secure POS and payment gateways with EMV, point-to-point encryption (P2PE), and tokenization, (3) segment and secure networks, (4) complete the Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) annually and conduct quarterly vulnerability scans, and (5) train employees on security protocols.

Tokenization replaces sensitive card data with unique tokens, reducing PCI audit scope and improving security. Common pitfalls include using outdated terminals, storing full card numbers or CVVs, not segmenting networks, failing to complete the SAQ, and assuming ecommerce platforms handle all PCI compliance.

# POS Terminal Import Guide: CE, FCC, EMV, PCI, VISA, Other Certifications You Need

2025-05-01    Author : ZCS

In the rapidly growing digital payments ecosystem, the demand for reliable and secure POS terminals is at an all-time high. Whether you're running a mobile point of sale system or managing a full-fledged supermarket POS system, certifications play a vital role in ensuring your POS terminals comply with international safety, interoperability, and security standards. This guide offers a comprehensive look into the key certifications you should look for when importing a POS terminal.

[**Why Certifications Matter in POS Terminals？**](https://www.szzcs.com/products/-POS-Terminal/z91-android-110-pos-doyhiw-hniwjt.html)

POS terminals are more than just hardware—they are the lifeblood of digital transactions. Without proper certifications, these systems may not meet security requirements, fail compliance audits, or even get rejected by payment networks. Certifications reassure both merchants and customers that transactions are safe, secure, and seamless. From small ecommerce pos setups to robust business pos systems used in retail chains, certified terminals guarantee credibility.

### **Key Certifications to Look For**

**1. EMV Certification**

* EMV stands for Europay, Mastercard, and Visa. This international standard guarantees the security of chip card transactions. Terminals with EMV certification help reduce card-present fraud by authenticating cards and encrypting transaction data.
* Why it matters: A must-have for any credit card pos system.
* Reference: **[EMVCo Official Site](https://www.emvco.com)**

**2. PCI PTS (PIN Transaction Security)**

* Administered by the PCI Security Standards Council, this certification governs how cardholder data is protected at the hardware level.
* Why it matters: Essential for pos technology providers to demonstrate commitment to data protection.
* Reference: **[PCI SSC Website](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org)**

**3. VISA & Mastercard Certification**

* Both card networks require separate certifications for any device processing their transactions. VISA includes PayWave, and Mastercard includes PayPass—contactless payment technologies that are growing in popularity.
* Why it matters: Ensures interoperability with global payment networks.
* Reference: **[VISA Technology Partner](https://technologypartner.visa.com)**and Mastercard Developer.

**4. UnionPay Certification**

* For companies targeting the Chinese market, UnionPay certification is crucial. It ensures your point of sale equipment can handle UnionPay transactions securely.
* Why it matters: A non-negotiable for POS systems in Asia.
* Reference: **[UnionPay Technical Support](https://open.unionpay.com)**

**5. CE and FCC Certifications**

* CE (Europe) and FCC (USA) certify that your [POS hardware complies](https://www.szzcs.com/products/-POS-Terminal/z92-android-130-pos-eixfen-hniwjt.html) with essential safety and electromagnetic compatibility requirements.
* Why it matters: Required for import into European and U.S. markets.

**6. TQM, TMS Certifications**

* Total Quality Management (TQM) and Terminal Management Systems (TMS) indicate operational reliability and maintainability of POS systems.
* Why it matters: [Especially relevant for pos inventory system](https://www.szzcs.com/products/Desktop-POS/z100-android-110-pos-doyhiw.html) and large-scale supermarket pos system deployments.

### **Industries That Need Certified POS Systems**

* **- Retailers:** From large chains to boutique stores, certified systems like the best pos system for retail or pos system for convenience store ensure compliance and trust.
* **- Restaurants:** For high-volume, fast-paced environments, certifications help ensure smooth operations in pos for grocery store and restaurant pos scenarios.
* **- Salons & Spas:** Niche businesses benefit from solutions like salon pos system or salon point of sale for secure, tailored transactions.
* **- Ecommerce:** Even digital-first businesses integrating offline touchpoints use ecommerce pos systems that require certification.

### [**Selecting the Right Certified POS Terminal**](https://www.szzcs.com/products/Desktop-POS/z100-android-110-pos.html)

When choosing a POS terminal, it’s critical to ensure it includes all relevant certifications. Look for models from reliable pos companies that cater to a wide array of use cases:

* **- Mobile POS system:** Ideal for food trucks, pop-ups, or on-the-go retail.
* **- Business POS system:** Suited for brick-and-mortar stores requiring robust reporting.
* **- Grocery POS system:** Optimized for perishables and inventory tracking.
* **- Bar POS system:** Designed for fast-paced beverage services.
* **- EPOS machine:** Enhanced with electronic payment features.

A terminal like the [**ZCS Z90**](https://www.szzcs.com/products/-POS-Terminal/z90n.html), for example, is equipped to meet professional business demands with full certification coverage—though this guide applies broadly to similar industry-leading devices.

### **Benefits of Using Certified POS Systems**

* **- Security:** Certified devices adhere to the highest industry security standards.
* **- Compatibility:** Works seamlessly with multiple payment processors.
* **- Customer Trust:** Certified POS instills confidence in your clientele.
* **- Reduced Liability:** Certification can protect against legal or compliance penalties.

### **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)**

**Q1: What happens if a POS terminal doesn’t have EMV certification?**

A: It may lead to chargebacks or fraud liability falling on the merchant.

**Q2: Can I use a POS system without FCC certification in the U.S.?**

A: No, FCC compliance is legally required for electronic equipment imports.

**Q3: What’s the difference between PayPass and PayWave?**

A: PayPass is Mastercard’s contactless payment tech, while PayWave is VISA’s version.

**Q4: Is CE certification sufficient for use in North America?**

A: No, CE is for Europe. For North America, you need FCC certification.

**Q5: Do all POS terminals support UnionPay?**

A: Only those that are specifically certified and programmed for UnionPay.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Set of security requirements for card processors

The **Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard** (**PCI DSS**) is a global [data security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_security "Data security") standard that regulates how entities store, process, and transmit cardholder data (CHD) and/or sensitive authentication data (SAD). PCI DSS includes guidelines regarding components of organizations' technical and operational system that are related to such data.[[1]](#cite_note-Objectives-1) Cardholder Data refers to information including Primary Account Numbers (PAN), cardholder names, expiration dates, and service codes. Sensitive authentication data refers to information including "full track data (magnetic-stripe data or equivalent on a chip)," card verification codes, and PINs/PIN blocks.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) This standard is administered by the [Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_Card_Industry_Security_Standards_Council "Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council"), and its use is enforced by the major payment card brands. PCI DSS was created to improve and streamline the [security controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_controls "Security controls") organizations use when handling cardholder data and reduce [credit card fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_card_fraud "Credit card fraud"). These organizations, including merchants and service providers, must prove compliance to the PCI DSS through an assessment and validation process. The payment card brands issue fines and other penalties when merchants or service providers fail to prove compliance. Validation of compliance is performed annually or quarterly with a method suited to the organization's volume of transactions:[[3]](#cite_note-PCI_DSS-3)

* Self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ)
* Firm-specific [Internal Security Assessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Security_Assessor "Internal Security Assessor") (ISA)
* External [Qualified Security Assessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualified_Security_Assessor "Qualified Security Assessor") (QSA)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Before the PCI DSS was launched, payment card information security was handled by the five major payment card brands: [Visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_Inc. "Visa Inc."), [Mastercard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastercard "Mastercard"), [American Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Express "American Express"), [Discover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discover_Card "Discover Card"), and [JCB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCB_(credit_card_company) "JCB (credit card company)").[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) They each had different independent security programs:[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)

* Visa's Cardholder Information Security Program[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)
* Mastercard's Site Data Protection[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)
* American Express's Data Security Operating Policy[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)
* Discover's Information Security and Compliance[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)
* JCB's Data Security Program[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)

The intentions of each were roughly similar: to create an additional level of protection for card issuers by ensuring that merchants meet minimum levels of security when they handle payment cards and related account information. As payment card fraud rose in the late 1990s and early 2000s,[[8]](#cite_note-8) the major payment card brands felt a growing need to streamline and unify these information security standards.[[9]](#cite_note-:3-9) Each program had its own methods and guidance regarding compliance validation, assessments, and requirements.[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6) To address interoperability problems among the existing standards, the combined effort by these payment card brands resulted in the release of version 1.0 of PCI DSS in December 2004.[[9]](#cite_note-:3-9) The main payment card brands then founded the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC)[[10]](#cite_note-:11-10) and aligned their policies to create the PCI DSS.[[11]](#cite_note-11) PCI DSS has since been implemented and followed by numerous organizations around the world.[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)

MasterCard, American Express, Visa, JCB International and Discover Financial Services established the PCI SSC in September 2006 as a global administrative and governing entity that mandates the evolution and development of the PCI DSS.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Independent private organizations can also participate in PCI development as part of the PCI Security Standards Council Participating Organization Program. To join that program, organizations must register as a PCI SSC Participating Organization (PO). Each participating organization joins a SIG (Special Interest Group) and contributes to activities mandated by the group.

The PCI DSS is a [living document](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_document "Living document") that is regularly updated by the PCI Security Standards Council. The PCI SSC releases major version updates, such as version 4.0, approximately every few years. Minor updates, such as version 4.0.1, are released more frequently and typically add small changes or clarifications.[[13]](#cite_note-:4-13) When updates are released, organizations have a transition period during which they must become familiar with the new changes and begin ensuring compliance with the current version.[[13]](#cite_note-:4-13) During the transition period, organizations are only required to be compliant with either the current version or the previous version.[[14]](#cite_note-14) The following versions of the PCI DSS have been made available:[[15]](#cite_note-PCIDSSLibrary-15)

| Version | Date | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0 | December 15, 2004 |
| 1.1 | September 2006 | clarification and minor revisions |
| 1.2 | October 2008 | enhanced clarity, improved flexibility, and addressed evolving risks and threats |
| 1.2.1 | July 2009 | minor corrections designed to create more clarity and consistency among the standards and supporting documents |
| 2.0 | October 2010 | provided clarifications about the relationship between PCI DSS and [PA-DSS (The Payment Application Data Security Standard)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PA-DSS "PA-DSS"), several additional guidelines regarding Requirement and Testing Procedure[[16]](#cite_note-16) |
| 3.0 | November 2013 | active from January 1, 2014 to June 30, 2015 |
| 3.1 | April 2015 | retired since October 31, 2016 |
| 3.2 | April 2016 | retired since December 31, 2018 |
| 3.2.1 | May 2018 | retired since March 31, 2024 |
| 4.0 | March 2022 | retired since December 31, 2024,[[17]](#cite_note-17) the biggest update and revision since v1.0[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5): updated firewall terminology, expansion of Requirement 8 to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA), increased flexibility to demonstrate security, and targeted risk analyses to establish risk exposure operation and management[[18]](#cite_note-18) |
| 4.0.1 | June 2024 | **Currently, the only active version.**[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[15]](#cite_note-PCIDSSLibrary-15) The deadline for compliance with this version was March 31, 2025.[[20]](#cite_note-20) minor revisions: correct typographical and other minor errors, update and clarify guidance, remove *Definitions* in guidance and refer to the Glossary instead, add references to the Glossary for newly defined glossary terms and for existing glossary terms that did not previously have references [[21]](#cite_note-:1-21) |

## Requirements and control objectives

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Requirements and control objectives")]

The PCI DSS has twelve requirements for compliance, organized into six related groups known as control objectives:[[1]](#cite_note-Objectives-1)

1. Build and maintain a [secure network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security "Transport Layer Security") and systems
2. Protect cardholder data
3. Maintain a vulnerability management program
4. Implement strong [access control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Access_control "Access control") measures
5. Regularly monitor and test networks
6. Maintain an information security policy

Each PCI DSS version has divided these six requirement groups differently, but the twelve requirements have not changed since the inception of the standard. Each requirement and sub-requirement is divided into three sections:

1. PCI DSS requirements: Define the requirement. The PCI DSS endorsement is made when the requirement is implemented.
2. Testing: The processes and methodologies carried out by the assessor for the confirmation of proper implementation.
3. Guidance: Explains the purpose of the requirement and the corresponding content, which can assist in its proper definition.

In version 4.0.1 of the PCI DSS, the twelve requirements are:[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

1. Install and maintain [network security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_security "Network security") controls.
2. Apply secure configurations to all system components.
3. Protect stored account data.
4. Protect cardholder data with [strong cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_cryptography "Strong cryptography") during transmission over open, public networks.
5. Protect all systems and networks from [malicious software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malware "Malware").
6. Develop and maintain secure systems and software.
7. Restrict access to system components and cardholder data by business [need to know](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Need_to_know "Need to know").
8. Identify users and [authenticate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authentication "Authentication") access to system components.
9. Restrict physical access to cardholder data.
10. Log and monitor all access to system components and cardholder data.
11. Test security of systems and networks regularly.
12. Support [information security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_security "Information security") with organizational policies and programs.

## Merchant levels

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Merchant levels")]

Merchants that store, process, and transmit cardholder data are subject to PCI DSS standards, and thus, must be deemed PCI-compliant. The PCI DSS framework classifies these entities into merchant levels that determine the type of reporting a business must complete to achieve compliance.[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6) A business' merchant level is determined by its dataset size which refers to the number of transactions a business makes annually.[[24]](#cite_note-24) An [acquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquiring_bank "Acquiring bank") or payment brand may manually place an organization into a reporting level at its discretion.[[25]](#cite_note-25) Not all payment card brands use all four merchant levels, and each level's transaction volume can vary among payment card brands.[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4) For instance, Visa only has three merchant levels.[[26]](#cite_note-:8-26) The four typically accepted merchant levels are:[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4)[[6]](#cite_note-:7-6)

* Level 1 – Over six million transactions annually
* Level 2 – Between one and six million transactions annually
* Level 3 – Between 20,000 and one million transactions annually, and all e-commerce merchants
* Level 4 – Less than 20,000 transactions annually

Each [card issuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_issuer "Card issuer") maintains a table of compliance levels and a table for service providers.[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)

## Service provider levels

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Service provider levels")]

According to the PCI DSS, third-party service providers that store, process, or transmit cardholder data, or have access to customers’ account data are subject to PCI DSS standards.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Service providers can include payment software vendors, [software as a service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service "Software as a service") (SaaS), [data centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_center "Data center"), and other such entities.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Service providers are required to prove PCI DSS compliance through the assessment process. The type of reporting process a service provider must complete are dependent on the type of service provider.[[10]](#cite_note-:11-10) Service providers are classified into levels which determine the reporting required for compliance.[[29]](#cite_note-:12-29) The two service provider levels are:[[29]](#cite_note-:12-29)

* Level 1:
  + All Third-Party Processors (TPPs)
  + All Staged Digital Wallet Operators (SDWOs)
  + All Digital Activity Service Providers (DASPs)
  + All Business Payment Service Providers (BPSPs)
  + All Token Service Providers (TSPs)
  + All [3-D Secure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-D_Secure "3-D Secure") Service Providers (3-DSSPs)
  + All Installment Service Providers (ISPs)
  + All Merchant Payment Gateways (MPGs)
  + All AML/Sanctions Service Providers, Data Storage Entities (DSEs) and Payment Facilitators (PFs) with more than 300,000 total combined Mastercard and Maestro transactions annually

* Level 2:
  + All AML/Sanctions Service Providers, DSEs6 and PFs with 300,000 or less total combined Mastercard and Maestro transactions annually
  + All Terminal Servicers (TSs)

## Compliance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Compliance")]

The payment card brands regularly require both merchants and service providers to demonstrate PCI DSS compliance.[[26]](#cite_note-:8-26) PCI DSS compliance involves implementing security controls that follow all requirements of the PCI DSS and passing the PCI DSS assessment process to achieve compliance validation.[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4) The major credit card brands enforce PCI DSS compliance[[4]](#cite_note-:5-4) by issuing fines for merchants who do not obtain compliance validation.[[30]](#cite_note-30) Merchants and service providers sign business-to-business contracts with payment processors and payment card brands, which outline such fines and fees.[[5]](#cite_note-:6-5) In the event of a merchant's compliance violation, payment card brands issue fines to the acquiring bank who then fines or otherwise penalizes the non-compliant merchant.[[31]](#cite_note-:9-31) Obtaining PCI DSS compliance and navigating the assessment process can be complicated, which is why many businesses often struggle with this. According to Verizon's 2018 Payment Security Report, 47.5% of organizations were not PCI DSS compliant during interim compliance validation. The number of organizations achieving compliance had been steadily increasing through the early 2010s, but this increase may likely have dropped in recent years.[[32]](#cite_note-32)

### Compliance validation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Compliance validation")]

Compliance validation involves the evaluation and confirmation that the security controls and procedures have been implemented according to the PCI DSS. Validation occurs through an annual assessment, either by an external entity, or by self-assessment.[[33]](#cite_note-PCI_Validation-33) The assessment process includes the following steps:[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

1. Confirm the scope of the PCI DSS assessment.
2. Perform the PCI DSS assessment of the environment.
3. Complete the applicable report for the assessment according to PCI DSS guidance and instructions.
4. Complete the Attestation of Compliance for Service Providers or Merchants, as applicable, in its entirety.
5. Submit the applicable PCI SSC documentation and the Attestation of Compliance, along with any other requested documentation to the requesting organization (those that manage compliance programs such as payment brands and acquirers (for merchants), or other requesters (for service providers)).

#### Report on Compliance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Report on Compliance")]

A Report on Compliance (ROC) is conducted by a PCI Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) and is intended to provide independent validation of an entity's compliance with the PCI DSS standard. A completed ROC results in two documents: a ROC Reporting Template populated with detailed explanation of the testing completed, and an Attestation of Compliance (AOC) documenting that a ROC has been completed and the overall conclusion of the ROC.

#### Self-Assessment Questionnaire

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Self-Assessment Questionnaire")]

The PCI DSS Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) is a validation tool intended for small to medium sized merchants and service providers to assess their own PCI DSS compliance status. There are multiple types of SAQ, each with a different length depending on the entity type and payment model used. Each SAQ question has a yes-or-no answer, and any "no" response requires the entity to indicate its future implementation. As with ROCs, an attestation of compliance (AOC) based on the SAQ is also completed.

#### Security Assessors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Security Assessors")]

The PCI Security Standards Council maintains a program to certify companies and individuals to perform assessment activities.

##### Qualified Security Assessor

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Qualified Security Assessor")]

A [Qualified Security Assessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualified_Security_Assessor "Qualified Security Assessor") (QSA) is an individual certified by the PCI Security Standards Council to validate another entity's PCI DSS compliance. QSAs must be employed and sponsored by a QSA Company, which also must be certified by the PCI Security Standards Council.[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)

##### Internal Security Assessor

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Internal Security Assessor")]

An [Internal Security Assessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Security_Assessor "Internal Security Assessor") (ISA) is an individual who has earned a certificate from the PCI Security Standards Council for their sponsoring organization, and can conduct PCI self-assessments for their organization. The ISA program was designed to help Level 2 merchants meet Mastercard compliance validation requirements.[[36]](#cite_note-FierceRetail_2010-36) ISA certification empowers an individual to conduct an appraisal of his or her association and propose security solutions and controls for PCI DSS compliance. ISAs are in charge of cooperation and participation with QSAs.[[33]](#cite_note-PCI_Validation-33)

## Compliance versus validation of compliance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Compliance versus validation of compliance")]

Although the PCI DSS must be implemented by all entities which process, store or transmit cardholder data and/or sensitive authentication data or could impact the security of such information,[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) formal validation of PCI DSS compliance is not mandatory for all entities. [Visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_Inc. "Visa Inc.") and [Mastercard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastercard "Mastercard") require merchants and service providers to be validated according to the PCI DSS; Visa also offers a Technology Innovation Program (TIP), an alternative program which allows qualified merchants to discontinue the annual PCI DSS validation assessment. Merchants are eligible if they take alternative precautions against fraud, such as the use of [EMV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMV "EMV") or [point-to-point encryption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-to-point_encryption "Point-to-point encryption").

[Issuing banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issuing_bank "Issuing bank") are not required to undergo PCI DSS validation, although they must secure sensitive data in a PCI DSS-compliant manner. Acquiring banks must comply with PCI DSS and have their compliance validated with an [audit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audit "Audit"). In a security breach, any compromised entity which was not PCI DSS-compliant at the time of the breach may be subject to additional penalties (such as fines) from card brands or acquiring banks.

## Legal status

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Legal status")]

No governing body/agency requires or enforces PCI DSS compliance, but if any PCI DSS requirements conflict with country, state, or local law, the law will apply.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) The European Union’s (EU) [General Data Protection Regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation "General Data Protection Regulation") (GDPR) is a legislative standard governing personal data. GDPR has similar security control standards as PCI DSS in regards to cardholder data because cardholder data is considered a form of personal data under GDPR.[[37]](#cite_note-:10-37) Hence, for many European organizations, a PCI DSS breach often constitutes a GDPR breach as well, which can result in fines from both major payment card brands and the European Union.[[31]](#cite_note-:9-31)[[37]](#cite_note-:10-37) These GDPR fines can be up to "€20 million or 4% of annual global turnover" (whichever is greatest).[[31]](#cite_note-:9-31)

### Legislation in the United States

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Legislation in the United States")]

While compliance with PCI DSS is not required by federal law in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"),[[38]](#cite_note-38) the laws of some US states refer to PCI DSS directly or make equivalent provisions. In 2007, [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota") enacted a law prohibiting the retention of some types of payment-card data more than 48 hours after authorization of a transaction.[[39]](#cite_note-39)[[40]](#cite_note-40) [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada") incorporated the standard into state law two years later, requiring compliance by merchants doing business in that state with the current PCI DSS and shielding compliant entities from liability. The Nevada law also allows merchants to avoid liability by other approved security standards.[[41]](#cite_note-41)[[42]](#cite_note-morse-42) In 2010, [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)") also incorporated the standard into state law. Unlike Nevada's law, entities are not required to be PCI DSS-compliant; however, compliant entities are shielded from liability in the event of a data breach.[[43]](#cite_note-43)[[42]](#cite_note-morse-42) Legal scholars Edward Morse and Vasant Raval have said that by enshrining PCI DSS compliance in legislation, card networks reallocated the cost of fraud from card issuers to merchants.[[42]](#cite_note-morse-42)

## Controversy and criticism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Controversy and criticism")]

The major payment card brands impose fines for non-compliance. Some business owners, small business owners especially,[[44]](#cite_note-44) criticize the PCI DSS system because the payment card brands impose fines on businesses even if no fraud occurs. Stephen and Theodora "Cissy" McComb, owners of a small restaurant called Cisero's Ristorante and Nightclub in [Park City, Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_City,_Utah "Park City, Utah"), were fined for a breach for which two forensics firms could not find evidence. They claim the PCI DSS system exists primarily for major card brands to extract profit from these merchant companies rather than ensure cardholder data security.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

Michael Jones, who was [CIO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_information_officer "Chief information officer") of [Michaels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaels "Michaels") at the time, testified before a US Congressional subcommittee about the PCI DSS:[[46]](#cite_note-46)

> [The PCI DSS requirements] are very expensive to implement, confusing to comply with, and ultimately subjective, both in their interpretation and in their enforcement. It is often stated that there are only twelve "Requirements" for PCI compliance. In fact there are over 220 sub-requirements; some of which can place an *incredible burden on a retailer* and *many of which are subject to interpretation*.

Proponents of the PCI DSS maintain that the PCI DSS may compel businesses to pay more attention to IT security, even if minimum standards are not enough to eradicate security problems. [Bruce Schneier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Schneier "Bruce Schneier") spoke in favor of the standard:

> Regulation—SOX, [HIPAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Insurance_Portability_and_Accountability_Act "Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act"), GLBA, the credit-card industry's PCI, the various disclosure laws, the European Data Protection Act, whatever—has been the best stick the industry has found to beat companies over the head with. And it works. Regulation forces companies to take security more seriously, and sells more products and services.[[47]](#cite_note-47)

[PCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payment_card_industry "Payment card industry") Council general manager Bob Russo responded to objections by the [National Retail Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Retail_Federation "National Retail Federation"):

> [PCI is a structured] blend ... [of] specificity and high-level concepts [that allows] stakeholders the opportunity and flexibility to work with Qualified Security Assessors (QSAs) to determine appropriate security controls within their environment that meet the intent of the PCI standards.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

Former Visa chief enterprise risk officer Ellen Richey said in 2018, "No compromised entity has yet been found to be in compliance with PCI DSS at the time of a breach".[[49]](#cite_note-COMPUTERWORLD--Post-breach-PCI-49) However, a 2008 breach of [Heartland Payment Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartland_Payment_Systems#Security_breach "Heartland Payment Systems") (validated as PCI DSS-compliant) resulted in the compromising of more than one hundred million card numbers.[[50]](#cite_note-:2-50) Around that time, [Hannaford Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannaford_Brothers_Company "Hannaford Brothers Company") and [TJX Companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TJX_Companies "TJX Companies") (also validated as PCI DSS-compliant) were similarly breached as a result of the allegedly-coordinated efforts of [Albert Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Gonzalez "Albert Gonzalez") and two unnamed Russian hackers.[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[50]](#cite_note-:2-50) In December 2013, more than forty million Target customer accounts were compromised in a data breach.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[50]](#cite_note-:2-50) Target’s Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer at the time John Mulligan confirmed that Target was certified PCI compliant months before the breach in September 2013.[[53]](#cite_note-53) News of incidents was widespread and called into question the adequacy of the PCI DSS.

Assessments examine the compliance of merchants and service providers with the PCI DSS at a specific point in time, frequently using [sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(statistics) "Sampling (statistics)") to allow compliance to be demonstrated with representative systems and processes. It is the responsibility of the merchant and service provider to achieve, demonstrate, and maintain compliance throughout the annual validation-and-assessment cycle across all systems and processes. A breakdown in merchant and service-provider compliance with the written standard may have been responsible for the breaches; Hannaford Brothers received its PCI DSS compliance validation one day after it had been made aware of a two-month-long compromise of its internal systems.

Compliance validation is required only for level 1 to 3 merchants and may be optional for Level 4, depending on the card brand and acquirer. According to Visa's compliance validation details for merchants, level-4 merchant compliance-validation requirements ("Merchants processing less than 20,000 Visa e-commerce transactions annually and all other merchants processing up to 1 million Visa transactions annually") are set by the [acquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquiring_bank "Acquiring bank"). Over 80 percent of payment-card compromises between 2005 and 2007 affected level-4 merchants, who handled 32 percent of all such transactions.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

args.summary:
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is a global data security standard administered by the Payment Card Industry Security Standards Council (PCI SSC) that regulates how entities store, process, and transmit cardholder data (CHD) and sensitive authentication data (SAD). It was created by the five major payment card brands (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, and JCB) to streamline security controls and reduce credit card fraud. The first version (1.0) was released in December 2004, and the PCI SSC was established in September 2006. The current active version is 4.0.1 (released June 2024), with a compliance deadline of March 31, 2025.

The standard has 12 requirements organized into 6 control objectives: build and maintain secure networks, protect cardholder data, maintain a vulnerability management program, implement strong access control measures, regularly monitor and test networks, and maintain an information security policy. The 12 requirements include installing network security controls, applying secure configurations, protecting stored account data, using strong cryptography, protecting against malware, developing secure systems, restricting access by need-to-know, authenticating users, restricting physical access, logging and monitoring access, testing security regularly, and maintaining information security policies.

Merchants are classified into four levels based on transaction volume (Level 1: over 6 million annually, down to Level 4: less than 20,000 annually). Service providers have two levels. Compliance validation can be done through Self-Assessment Questionnaires (SAQ), Internal Security Assessors (ISA), or external Qualified Security Assessors (QSA).

PCI DSS is not federal law in the US, though some states have incorporated it into legislation. In the EU, PCI DSS breaches often constitute GDPR breaches as well, with fines up to €20 million or 4% of annual global turnover. The standard has faced criticism for its cost and complexity, particularly for small businesses, and notable breaches occurred at Heartland Payment Systems, Hannaford Brothers, TJX Companies, and Target—all of which were PCI DSS-compliant at the time of their breaches.
